paras: The lynching of Sam Saxon took place on the night of Sunday, August 21, 1881, when an armed party of citizens took Saxon and a second Black prisoner from the jail at Orange, Texas, and shot them both dead. Saxon had surrendered that morning, accused of drawing Sheriff George Michael into an ambush four days earlier, after which his brother Robert had been hanged and other Black men shot. The killings drew national coverage and a Black protest meeting in Galveston.

According to the Houston wire, the trouble began when a detective shot O. L. Delno and Delno's brother Charles accused Sheriff Michael of helping the detective escape. A Globe-Democrat dispatch described instead a six-year feud between the townsmen and a party led by Charles Delano whose followers included the brothers Robert and Sam Saxon.

On the night of Wednesday, August 17, Sam Saxon and other Black men reportedly assaulted a white man, Gus Garvey, in a saloon. Sheriff Michael and a small posse followed them toward 'negro town', where, by the Orange Tribune's account, they were fired on from ambush and Michael was wounded. About 150 armed citizens took up the pursuit, and by the next morning Robert Saxon was hanging from the oak in front of D. Call & Son's store, with others killed or wounded. Delano, a white man, was jailed as an alleged instigator, and the Orange Rifles guarded the jail.

Sam Saxon gave himself up about 9 o'clock on Sunday morning and was placed in the jail. About 8 o'clock that evening the Orange Rifles disbanded, leaving the jail unguarded. An hour later an armed party, about 20 men by the Ottawa Free Trader's count and thirty by a Globe-Democrat dispatch, surrounded the jail. Deputy Sheriff Rance Jett, in charge, judged resistance useless and yielded the jail.

The party took out Saxon and another Black prisoner, described only as his 'leading accomplice'. Saxon fell to his knees and clung to the deputy's legs, begging for mercy. By differing accounts they broke and ran or their yells exasperated the citizens; both were shot with buckshot and left where they fell.

Delano was to face a 'Kangaroo court' on Monday and was expected to hang, but he was instead released on $2000 bond and prepared to leave the country. No report of an inquest or of any arrest for the two killings appears in the coverage.

Governor Roberts declined a request for troops. On August 24 a meeting of 300 Black residents of Galveston denounced the 'outrages perpetrated on negroes' at Orange and the governor's refusal to interfere. Its resolutions, reported in Wisconsin, condemned 'the butchery of innocent negroes by the mob at Orange'.

A Houston special to the St. Louis Republican ran on August 23 and 24 in papers from Washington to Chicago and Savannah. It presented the citizens' ambush story as fact and repeated a confession attributed to Saxon. The Wheeling Intelligencer's headline 'Halter and Pistol' praised a mob 'Determined to Put an End to Wild Lawlessness', while the New-York Tribune wrote that citizens 'Fight Lawlessness with Lawlessness'.

Near Orange, the Orange Tribune called the earlier killings 'a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community', and a New Orleans Times special wrote that 'forbearance is no longer a virtue'. In Illinois the Ottawa Free Trader credited 'the decent people of the town'.

The sharpest dissent was a Globe-Democrat dispatch printed in the Omaha Bee, which said the ambush story came from Michael's party and had not been established, and quoted witnesses that the prisoners were 'shot down like dogs'. The Houston Post, quoted in the San Marcos Free Press, said excitement could not justify the violence, but chiefly objected that 'Negroes who surrendered were shot down' while Delano went free on bail.

A New Orleans Times special named the man taken from the jail as Bob Saxon and put the time near midnight, but the correspondents at Orange named Sam Saxon, gave 9 o'clock, and placed Bob's hanging on August 18. Saxon's confession, implicating Delano and a woman said to have offered him $500 to burn the town, was reported only from the lynchers' side.

reader.title: Lynching of Sam Saxon
bases: An armed party of citizens took Sam Saxon and another Black prisoner from the Orange jail after the deputy in charge yielded it, and shot both dead (A5, A13, A17).

Two Black prisoners were taken from jail and shot by a party of about 20 (A14) to thirty (A19) armed men with no legal authority, in response to the alleged plot against Sheriff Michael and to end 'lawlessness' (A5, A17).

The Galveston News correspondence (A17), the New Orleans Democrat special from Orange (A13), the Houston wire (A5, A6) and the Globe-Democrat dispatch (A19) independently agree that Saxon and another Black prisoner were taken from the jail on Sunday night and shot.

accounts.label: New Orleans Times special
accounts.gist: Bob Saxon, said to have shot the sheriff, was arrested, and about midnight a band broke open the jail and shot him and another negro.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat dispatch from Houston
accounts.gist: The ambush by negroes was claimed by Michael's party but not established; eyewitnesses said the prisoners clung to the officers' knees before a mob of thirty and were 'shot down like dogs'.

framing.detail: Wheeling's 'Halter and Pistol' ran the Houston wire under a subhead praising a mob 'Determined to Put an End to Wild Lawlessness' and reported that 'No sympathy whatever is expressed'.
The New-York Tribune headed the same wire 'Citizens Become Incensed and Fight Lawlessness with Lawlessness'.
The Chicago Tribune ran the Houston wire as 'A Reign of Terror'; the Savannah Morning News as 'Trouble in Texas'.
The New Orleans Times special called the dead 'negro roughs' and wrote that 'forbearance is no longer a virtue'.
The Orange Tribune called the killings 'a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community'.
The Ottawa Free Trader's 'Kangaroo Justice' credited 'the decent people of the town' with resolving to destroy the 'desperadoes'.
The Globe-Democrat dispatch called it a 'dreadful slaughter' of helpless men killed 'without a semblance of a trial'.
The Houston Post, quoted by the San Marcos Free Press, said excitement could not justify the violence but chiefly attacked the release of Delano while 'Negroes who surrendered were shot down'.

conflicts.note: The correspondents at Orange (A13, A17) and the Orange Tribune (A16) place Bob/Robert Saxon's hanging on the morning after the ambush, so Sam is the better-supported name.
The two reports written at Orange give 9 o'clock.
